Marathon Petroleum fell 3% today after a sharp reversal from Friday's peak of $414.65. The move follows news that Russian crude production has rebounded significantly following a diesel deal, pushing global oil markets into surplus—meaning supply is now outpacing demand. For a refiner, surplus crude is a double-edged sword: while cheaper oil helps processing costs, it narrows the profit margin between what they pay for crude and what they can sell refined products for, which is a core driver of refinery earnings.

The two-week decline of 6.5% reflects broader pressure on refining margins. Heating oil prices are up 59% from last winter, which sounds bullish for a refiner, but that headline actually signals tight supply and squeezed consumer demand—families cutting back on heating oil purchases because of cost. Meanwhile, U.S. refineries are running at 95.2% capacity with ample crude and product inventories, which suggests the market is well-stocked and demand growth is modest at best.
